newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - Bio-Vascular sees sales floor.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Bio-Vascular sees sales floor.

text.p: Bio-Vascular Inc expects to get at least $650,000 per year in U.S. revenues from its Peri-Strips for lung volume reduction surgery, even without a change in Medicare's reimbursement policy on the product.

In addition, chief executive John Karcanes said in an interview that non-U.S. Peri-Strip revenues in the next fiscal year "should approach...in rough terms between $4.5 and $5 million." The company's fiscal year ends October 31.
Karcanes said he is comfortable with fiscal 1996 results forecasts ranging from break-even to a $0.01 per share profit.

"I wish we could do better, but that's likely where we're going to end up, probably a penny positive," Karcanes said. Analysts' estimates for fiscal 1996 results range from $0.01 per share loss to $0.01 per share profit, First Call said.
In fiscal 1996, the St. Paul-based medical products maker had earnings of $0.27 per share on sales of $13.3 million.
Bio-Vascular was clobbered in January when the U.S. Health Care Financing Administration said lung volume reduction surgery was no longer eligible for Medicare reimbursement.
Sales of Peri-Strips plunged after the HCFA ruling to $1 million in the third quarter from $1.7 million a year before.
Lung volume reduction surgery is the only therapeutic alternative for late-stage emphysema patients to lung transplant, a risky procedure made more problematic by a chronic shortage of donor lungs.

Lung reduction involves cutting out diseased portions of an emphysema patient's lungs, then closing the tissue with surgical staples. Early results were hampered by leaks around the staples. But Peri-Strips -- a surgical staple backing made from cow pericardium -- solves the problem, Bio-Vascular said.
Introduced in late 1994, Peri-Strips proved widely popular among pulmonologists and sales soared.
Then federal regulators' attention focused on the costly surgery and Medicare reimbursement was withdrawn.

HCFA said it wanted to see the long-term results of the innovative surgery before approving it for reimbursement. Initially, Karcanes hoped for a turnaround on HCFA status of a few months. Now, he is less optimistic.

Regulators are planning a seven-year study. Karcanes said he is lobbying in Washington to have the length of the study reduced. But, he said, "I do think it's going to take two or three years...to get long-term data."
Third-party payors, such as private insurers and HMOs, continue to cover lung volume reduction surgery, despite HCFA's position, analysts said.

"It's not as though the procedure's been banned, but without Medicare, the majority of patients who could benefit from this procedure are without recourse," said Principal Financial analyst Mark Kelliher.

Meanwhile, Bio-Vascular is adjusting. "I think we'll show pretty healthy revenue growth and reasonable profitability in fiscal '97," Karcanes said. "We've got long-term value through other tissue guard applications and the imaging business."

In addition to Peri-Strips, Bio-Vascular sells tissue patches for the brain, the peripheral vascular system and other uses, two surgical tools and a three-dimensional medical imaging software called VoxelView.

These technologies and projects in the research pipeline show promise, said R.J. Steichen healthcare analyst Edward Higgins. "My problem with the stock is I don't see anything short-term that's going to move it," he said.
